sections.heading: GeM Registration Charges 2026: Is It Really Free? Breaking Down the Costs
paragraphs: Ask ten people if GeM registration is free, and nine of them will say yes without blinking. Technically, they're right. The government doesn't charge you a rupee to open a seller account on the Government e-Marketplace. No signup fee. No membership card. No hidden "processing charge" tucked into a form.

But here's the catch nobody mentions in the first thirty seconds of that answer: registering is free. Selling isn't always free. Once you actually start doing business on GeM, a few costs quietly show up, including some mandatory, some optional, and some that depend entirely on how big your business is. If you walked in expecting zero costs forever, you'd be in for a small surprise a few months in.
So let's actually break this down. No fluff, no vague "terms and conditions apply."Just the real numbers, where they come from, and who has to pay them.

Yes. Creating your account on gem.gov.in costs nothing. You sign up, verify your Aadhaar or PAN, and fill in your business details, and that's it. There’s no government fee at any point in that process.

This applies whether you're registering as a manufacturer, a service provider, or an authorised reseller. The Government of India built GeM to make procurement easier and more transparent, and part of that promise means keeping the entry point open to anyone who qualifies, regardless of company size.

So why does the "is GeM free" question even keep coming up? Because people confuse ‘registration’ with ‘operating’. Those are two very different things. Think of it like opening a shop in a market. The stall might be free to set up, but you still pay for electricity, security, and maybe a cut to the market association once you start earning. GeM works on similar logic. And this is something that a professional GeM registration service provider will let you know at the start.

This is where things get a little more interesting and also a little more confusing, honestly, because not every source online agrees on the exact numbers. Here's what you actually need to know after your GeM registration online.

Caution money is a refundable deposit some sellers are asked to pay once their turnover crosses a certain point. Most sources describe a slab system based on annual turnover, roughly along these lines:
Turnover under ₹1 crore — around ₹5,000
Turnover between ₹1 crore and ₹10 crore — around ₹10,000
Turnover above ₹10 crore — around ₹25,000

Here's the honest part: there's genuine disagreement right now about whether this system is still active. Some recent reports say GeM has moved away from caution money entirely and replaced it with a different, usage-based charge instead. Others say the slab system is still very much in use. Rather than pretend there's one clean answer, the smart move is to check the Seller Corner on gem.gov.in directly before you budget for this. GeM's revenue policy has been updated more than once, and what was true last year might not be true today.
One thing almost everyone agrees on, though, is that certain sellers are exempt from caution money altogether. More on that later.

GeM tracks something called Seller Merchandise Value, or SMV. It's simply the total value of orders you've completed in a financial year. Once your SMV crosses a threshold, GeM starts applying a transaction charge, usually calculated as a small percentage of the order value.

Picture it this way: you're not paying anything on your first few orders. But once your combined sales for the year cross that line, GeM takes a small cut on new orders going forward. The percentage tends to shrink as your order size grows into the crores. It's not a flat rate across the board.
